deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page is part of Gauss's Hanover triangulation of 1824. The previous page adjusted the 1824 directions station by station, without regard to the side conditions (Seitenverhaeltnisse). Its station numbers fix the labels used here: 1 Wilsede, 2 Elmhorst, 3 Litberg, 4 Bullerberg, 5 Bruettendorf, 6 Zeven, 7 Bottel, 8 Steinberg, 9 Bremen. On this page the unknown (ij) is a further correction, in arc seconds, to the azimuth of line i-j. Because the azimuth i->j and the azimuth j->i differ by 180 deg, one correction serves both ends of the line. The goal is to choose these (ij) so that the sine (side) conditions of the polygons are satisfied exactly.

A. SIDE CONDITIONS (Bedingungsgleichungen). For a closed figure with a central point, going round the figure from side to side by the sine rule must return the starting side. In logarithms: sum log sin(group 1 angles) - sum log sin(group 2 angles) = 0.
- Each angle is given with its value, log10 sin, and the tabular difference per 1 arc second in units of 1e-7 of the log. That difference is D = 1e7*M*cot(x)/rho'' = 21.055*cot(x), with M = log10(e) and rho'' = 206264.8.
- My checks of D: 6d4'29.4'' gives 197.8; 4d42'30'' gives 255.7; 3d27'46'' gives 347.9.
- The misclosure w is Sigma1 - Sigma2 in units of 1e-7. My recomputation:
  - Quadrilateral 1356: 28.7238677 - 28.7238774 = -97.
  - Quadrilateral 1457: -76; Gauss writes +76, presumably the opposite orientation (signs of the coefficients not checked).
  - Pentagon 12345 (condition c): +27.
  - Pentagon 15679: -300; Gauss writes +300, again opposite orientation.
  - Pentagon 15789: -396.
  - Pentagon 56789: -4 (he writes -4, strikes it, but carries -4,0000 in the elimination).
- Each angle is a difference of two line azimuths. The coefficient of (ij) is therefore a signed sum of the D's of the angles in which line ij occurs. I checked them, for example:
  - Condition 1: (15) = 1.3 + 255.7 = 257.0; (16) = -(36.3 + 255.7) = -292.0; (35) = -(197.8 + 22.9); (36) = 197.8 + 6.7; (56) = 22.9 - 1.3 = 21.6.
  - Condition 4: (59) = -(347.9 + 23.6) = -371.5; (69) = 347.9 + 28.9 = 376.8.
  - Condition 5: (17) = -(34.2 + 249.7); (18) = 249.7 + 13.9.
- The six linear conditions are w_k + sum_ij A_k,ij (ij) = 0, with correlates a, b, c, d, e, f for k = 1..6.

B. CORRELATE EXPRESSIONS. Minimising sum p_ij (ij)^2 subject to the six conditions gives (ij) = (1/p_ij) * sum_k A_k,ij k. Gauss lists the 21 corrections (12) ... (89) as linear forms in a ... f.
- (56) and (78) carry an asterisk. Their squares and products enter the normal equations multiplied by 4, i.e. weight 1/4. My examples: 43.2^2 = 1866.24 is entered in place of 21.6^2; 4*29.3^2 = 3433.96; 4*3.3^2 = 43.56; 4*3.0^2 = 36.00.
- These are the two very short lines, Bruettendorf-Zeven (log s = 3.58) and Bottel-Steinberg (log s = 3.67). On the previous page their entries are bracketed. My reading is that their azimuths are treated as 4 times less certain.

C. NORMAL EQUATIONS. [kl] = sum A_k A_l / p. Gauss gives every term and the sums: aa = 244584.14, ab = 28321.40, ac = 16214.33, ad = -151817.02, ae = 10382.80, af = -285.12, bb = 52785.02, bc = 6529.12, bd = -28776.36, be = -23239.98, bf = -949.52, cc = 6516.76, cd = -14871.87, ce = 2072.52, cf = 0, dd = 435524.09, de = -40965.11, df = 10346.00, ee = 206069.53, ef = -1389.50, ff = 1220.07. The absolute terms are -97, +76, +27, +300, -396, -4.

D. ELIMINATION. The reduction is done with logarithms and square roots.
- Block a: log aa = 5.38843 and its half 2.694215 = log sqrt(aa). For each other entry, log(ak) - log sqrt(aa) gives l_ka = [ak]/sqrt[aa]. The constant is treated the same way: q_a = -97/sqrt(aa), log 9.292555n.
- The reduced quantities are then [kl.1] = [kl] - l_ka*l_la. For example bb: 52785.02 - 3279.38 = 49505.64.
- This is repeated for b, c, d, e, f. The final diagonals are 49505.64, 5004.77, 335939.61, 186737.39 and 897.361. The final reduced constants are 87.2318, 25.233, 278.4558, -336.492 and -12.7240.
- In modern terms this is exactly the Cholesky (square-root) factorisation N = L L^T together with forward substitution L q = w. Every product l_ki*l_li is formed as a sum of logarithms.
- I recomputed every reduction step to the last figure, e.g. 10^(2*1.757895) = 3279.4; 10^(2.487105*2) = 94234; ef chain -1389.50 -> -762.41; q_f = -12.724/sqrt(897.361), log 9.628145n.
- The next page carries out the back substitution (f = +0.014179, ...), evaluates the (ij), and from them computes the coordinates.
errors: [be]: the term from (15) should be 110.2*40.4 = 4452.08. Gauss wrote 4448.04 (as if 110.1*40.4), so [be] = -23239.98 instead of -23236.94. The effect on the result is negligible.
[ef]: the term from the starred line (78) should be 4*(-16.1)*(-3.0) = 193.20. Gauss wrote 192.40, so [ef] = -1389.50 instead of -1388.70. This is a negligible slip.

Sign conventions: for conditions 2 and 4 my recomputed Sigma1 - Sigma2 is -76 and -300, while Gauss writes +76 and +300. This is presumably the opposite orientation, consistent with his coefficient signs, which I have not fully checked. It is not evidently an error.
Condition 6: the absolute term -4 is struck through on the page, yet -4,0000 is still used in the elimination (consistent with my recomputed misclosure of -4).
Apart from these, all checked log-sines, tabular differences, coefficient sums, normal-equation entries and every step of the logarithmic square-root elimination agree to the last figure.

results.what: Sine (side) conditions for the quadrilaterals 1356 and 1457 and the central pentagons 12345, 15679, 15789 and 56789, linearised via log-sine tabular differences in azimuth corrections
results.modern_name: side (sine) condition equations in triangulation adjustment
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Hanover survey practice, 1820s); also Legendre and Bessel for the geodetic conditions

results.what: Adjustment by correlates with weights (short lines given weight 1/4), forming the normal equations of the correlates
results.modern_name: least-squares adjustment of condition equations (method of correlates / Lagrange multipliers)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Theoria combinationis observationum (1821-23) and Supplementum (1826)

results.what: Solution of the 6x6 normal equations by dividing each row by sqrt of the pivot, done in logarithms: l_ki = [ki.(i-1)]/sqrt([ii.(i-1)]), with reduced [kl.i] = [kl.(i-1)] - l_ki*l_li
results.usually_credited_to: A.-L. Cholesky (c. 1910, published by Benoit 1924); Gauss is credited with the LDL^T form of the elimination

deep.surprise_reason: The adjustment itself is standard Gaussian geodesy of 1824, well documented as his. The mildly notable feature is the elimination: it is carried out in the symmetric square-root form, i.e. effectively the Cholesky factorisation, a natural choice when working with logarithms. That form is usually credited to Cholesky about 1910. Geodetic computers may well have used it informally, and I am unsure whether historians already attribute it to Gauss's hand computations, so the surprise is modest.

transcription_corrections: Condition 6: the absolute term '-4' is struck out ('0 = [-4-] 3,3(56) ...'), but -4,0000 is used in the .f column of the elimination.
In the af and cf boxes the entries are '-285,12' and '*' (cf = 0, no common line); cf appears as 0 in the elimination.
The column the machine transcription labels 'ee' (-367,396; -30,904; -336,492) is the continuation of the .e constant reduction; the true ee reduction starts at 206069,53.
The column the machine transcription labels 'ff' (-3,0276; +8,3226; -11,3502; +1,3738; -12,7240) is the continuation of the .f constant reduction.
The second-block 'bb: +76,00; -11,2318; +87,2318' is the .b constant reduction, not bb.
Asterisks mark (56) and (78): squares and products for these lines are multiplied by 4 (weight 1/4) in the normal equations.
